blocks.text: Memphis Jr. was the children's version of Memphis Design. It took the popular Memphis-Milano style created by the Italian architecture and design firm Memphis Group and applied it to storefronts, advertisements, and toys marketed towards young children. Memphis Jr. was most popular during the late 1980s to the mid 90s, until it was eventually replaced by newer child-focused aesthetics like Wacky Pomo.

Influenced by the eccentric forms and bold colors of Radical Design, this aesthetic is characterized by vibrant colors, geometric shapes, contrasting patterns on bright backgrounds, and patterns like stripes and squiggles.

Memphis Design was a widely praised design style from the 1980s, becoming prevalent internationally throughout the 80s and 90s. Its aesthetic dominance was not reseverved to public and commercial spaces -- private homes utilized Memphis Design too, through art pieces, furniture, and even the architecture of the building itself. It directly influenced later aesthetics such as Memphis Lite and Factory Pomo.

Memphis Jr. is an offshoot of this, taking the experimental, bright style and applying it to more kid-centric designs. This was a successful repurposing of the renowned Memphis look, as the bright colors and wacky shapes were easy to implement in children's marketing, capturing the attention and fascination of kids and adults alike.

As design advanced and trends changed, by the late 90s, Memphis Jr. fell out of popularity and was superseded by aesthetics like Wacky Pomo, Utopian Scholastic, and Preschool Pop. However, it was still used in some animated productions.

In the late 2010s, the term "Memphis Jr." (and its alternative name, "Playskool PoMo") was retroactively coined by architect and design archivist Evan Collins, and the team of design researchers at the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute.

Like its predecessor, Memphis Jr. is defined by its usage of bright colors and eye-catching patterns. Colors typical to this aesthetic are red, pink, purple, yellow, orange, and various shades of blue. Defined geometric shapes (squares, polka dots) are used side-by-side with more freeform or organic ones, such as waves, swirls, squiggly lines, and zig-zags. Stripes and checkerboards are common patterns, and can show up in contrasting colors, complementary colors, or in black-and-white. All of these designs are often placed on a white background to make them more striking.

There are a few patterns specific to Memphis design that often appear in Memphis Jr. as well, such as Bacterio, a pattern created by Ettore Sottsass, as well as the sprinkle/confetti version of Bacterio that is more consistent in form and shape. Alongside these, you will see visuals common to most child-centric aesthetics: large letters and numbers, stars, imagery of toys and mascots, bugs and animals, and representations of locations children are familiar with, such as school buildings, playgrounds, and homes.
